title: Plots, love letters and remedies: The medieval secrets being revealed by AI
facts: Researchers used machine learning to decode the 408-page Borg cipher manuscript from the Vatican library.
The Borg cipher manuscript was encoded using 34 obscure symbols alongside a few Roman letters.
Beáta Megyesi is a professor in computational linguistics at Stockholm University in Sweden.
Approximately 1% of the material in archives and libraries around the world is estimated to be encrypted.
Cecile Pierrot is a cryptologist at the French National Institute for Computer Science Research (INRIA).
Cecile Pierrot and colleagues decrypted a 500-year-old letter from Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.
Michelle Waldispühl is a professor of German linguistics at the University of Oslo in Norway.
Researchers used the Transkribus AI platform to transcribe a 1637 cipher letter by Sigismund Heusner von Wandersleben.
The multinational Descrypt project is developing an AI tool to convert handwritten historical ciphers into machine-readable text.
Researchers tested an AI transcription system on the 105-page Copiale cipher manuscript.
The Descrypt project compiled a database of historical cipher scripts, including 400 encrypted postcards.
Beáta Megyesi's team developed an AI chatbot tool that combines transcription and decryption in a single step.
The AI chatbot tool translated and decoded a 500-symbol extract of the Borg cipher in just over 29 minutes.
The Phaistos Disc from Crete is a 4,000-year-old artifact that remains undeciphered.
The ancient Greek script 'Linear A' remains undeciphered.
